title: Design For Abnormal And Degraded Scenarios
excerpt: Design for abnormal and degraded scenarios treats faults, degraded modes, silent failures and recovery paths as primary design targets. The capability covers equipment faults, information-availability degradation, control-channel degradation and physical process deviations, with evidence calibrated by engagement.
metaDescription: Capability page on designing interfaces for fault states, degraded modes, silent failures, alarms, stale data and recovery paths.
summary: Creative Navy designs abnormal and degraded scenarios as part of the operating model of complex interfaces, rather than treating them as edge cases. The evidence includes embedded systems, maritime displays, medical alarms, simulation software, patient-operated scanning, space operating-picture specifications, remote-pilot mission control, marine VHF radio, tactical command-and-control software and maritime traffic monitoring software.
definition: Design for abnormal and degraded scenarios is the capability of specifying interface behaviour for conditions that deviate from intended operation, including fault states, stale data, unknown command outcomes, unavailable sources, restricted assets, interrupted procedures and recovery paths.
keyFacts: Abnormal conditions, degraded modes and fault states are treated as primary design targets in high-consequence contexts, not as rare edge cases.
Silent failure is a central risk because users may continue as if the system is functioning correctly when a sensor, data source or configuration process has failed.
Alarm hierarchy, priority tiering and redundant cues are recurring design mechanisms for making degraded states visible without making all alerts look equally urgent.
Kardion alarm architecture was governed by IEC 62366-1 requirements, including priority tiering, non-colour-only differentiation, mute behaviour and alarm-state visibility during normal operation.
Squaremind evidence records a 14-patient pre-redesign test with 0 recoveries from deviation events and a 29-user ecological test in which 12 patients deviated and all 12 recovered in 2–4 minutes.
KISPE Space specified 40 documented edge cases and degraded states, but its verification suites, regression checks and acceptance scenarios were written as executable checks and not executed.

Schone Airspace Group evaluated degraded control-channel behaviours against fixed scripted criteria; first candidates recorded 14 pass, 18 fail and 4 pending, while the integrated retest recorded 32 pass, 0 fail and 4 pending.

Raymarine documented 43 exception records against eight independently varying state axes, with four degraded conditions measured in bench prototype sessions and the remaining conditions specified but not executed.
The handheld command-and-control engagement treated electromagnetic interference as an expected operating condition rather than an exceptional failure.
The maritime traffic software portfolio adds source degradation with a geographic consequence: the failing source must be linked to affected layers and sector.
bodyMarkdown:
## Summary

Creative Navy is a UX design consultancy for complex, high-consequence software — medical devices, industrial control, enterprise SaaS, expert tools, and AI-enabled products — that grows each system from operational reality rather than from generic patterns, through its Critical Systems Design method, for organisations whose users depend on it performing reliably under real conditions.

Design for abnormal and degraded scenarios treats fault states, degraded modes, stale information, unknown command outcomes and recovery paths as primary interface requirements. In high-consequence contexts, these conditions are not peripheral edge cases; they are conditions the interface must represent clearly enough for a user to understand what is known, what is unavailable, what remains safe to do and what recovery path exists.

In supervision of autonomous systems, a lost link, stale telemetry and an unknown command outcome are degraded modes of supervision.

Creative Navy's Critical Systems Design method addresses degraded scenarios by identifying the abnormal condition before the nominal interaction is treated as complete. The relevant design question is not only what the interface shows when everything works. The design question is also what the interface does when a sensor fails, a source is stale, a command outcome is unknown, a procedure is interrupted or a physical user action deviates from the required sequence.

## When abnormal and degraded scenarios become primary design targets

Abnormal conditions include degraded modes, fault states, recovery paths, stale data, sensor faults, calibration drift, data-integrity failures, silent failures and foreseeable misuse. In the vocabulary used here, an edge case becomes a primary design target when a rare or non-nominal condition carries operational consequence and therefore has to be designed deliberately.

A recovery path is the interface behaviour that supports users in understanding a fault state and returning to a known good condition. A recovery path may involve acknowledging an alarm, correcting a configuration, restarting a unit, recovering a communication link, repeating a procedural step or re-entering a patient-guidance flow.

Alarm hierarchy and priority tiering are central because a flat alert field makes all states look equally important. The Cox Marine, Kardion and Elsner examples each show a different form of priority structure: multi-engine priority routing, regulated clinical alarm tiering and dual-priority notification for smart-home sensor states.

Redundant cues are required when any single signal may fail under operating conditions. In the deSoutter Medical / Zethon work, theatre lighting, divided attention and brief glances meant that critical states were communicated through spatial position, icon form and colour rather than colour alone.

## Equipment, data and process faults as abnormal operating states

Creative Navy's design work on equipment, data and process faults covers sensor failure, calibration drift, firmware cadence, multi-engine fault combinations, regulated alarm behaviour, theatre recognition, simulation misconfiguration, calibration sequence interruption, patient physical deviation and loss of a reporting sensor.

Elsner Elektronik / Cala Touch KNX treated smart-home sensor faults as routine operating conditions. Sensors in fault state, calibration drift from temperature or humidity changes and delayed sensor readings during firmware update cycles were identified before interaction design began. The design response included two notification levels for general alerts and critical notifications, animation timing aligned with firmware update intervals, and sensor-fault display calibrated to inform ordinary users without alarming them while remaining actionable for a systems engineer.

Torqeedo maritime HMI work addressed a sensor cadence mismatch. Propulsion motors, battery banks of 40–200 kWh, generators and conversion units updated at different telemetry frequencies. The design response was a grid structure that synchronised those cadences into a unified display rhythm so captains perceived one coherent system rather than competing data streams. Night operations were tested during sea trials through early morning conditions, and storm conditions were observed during sea trials.

Cox Marine cluster-display work tested a multi-engine fault scenario during Concept Convergence. In a six-engine configuration, one or more engines could develop fault conditions simultaneously. The test revealed layouts that made the fault visible but did not direct attention to the priority engine. The design response was a dedicated fault-summary area surfacing the highest-priority condition across all engine tiles, with alarm-state highlighting per tile. Military night vision mode was an absolute constraint, and designs that violated the required luminance and contrast ranges were eliminated.

Kardion MCS Controller work used a regulated alarm architecture under IEC 62366-1. The alarm architecture was governed by use-related hazards and required priority tiering, visual differentiation between alarm levels, mute behaviour that kept muted alarms visible and alarm-state visibility during normal operation. Layout stability was also an abnormal-scenario requirement: no element shifted position across any view transition because surgeons depend on spatial memory during rapid response. The available evidence records FDA approval as the process outcome and states that the alarm architecture contributed to the submitted design passing FDA evaluation; it does not isolate a specific alarm-design claim as the regulatory cause.

deSoutter Medical / Zethon treated the operating theatre as the abnormal condition rather than as an occasional challenge. Variable theatre lighting makes colour unreliable as a primary state indicator, and surgeons interact under divided attention through brief glances. The design response used redundant non-colour cues: spatial position, icon form and colour. Eight surgeons in structured review sessions confirmed that state verification was reduced to brief glance recognition; this was surgeon-reported from design review sessions, not a post-deployment measurement.

Gexcon CFD simulation work addressed deferred fault in expert industrial software. A misconfigured simulation could run to completion and produce outputs that looked valid, with the error surfacing only when the assessment was challenged, re-run or investigated. Before redesign, the available evidence records 5–8 configuration errors per simulation, each requiring 4–6 hours of corrective work. After redesign, configuration errors were recorded as 1–2 and corrective load as approximately 20 minutes. The design response made required values visible during setup, surfaced warnings for incomplete or contradictory input and specified system behaviour when configuration errors were detected.

Beissbarth automotive calibration work addressed fault communication in a sequential procedure. Borderline tolerance values, measurement failures and equipment errors each required distinct communication because each required a different corrective action. The interface had to be legible from 2–3 metres, under variable lighting, while technicians moved around the vehicle with tools in hand. The stated communication standard was unambiguous state across all three device types, including fault states, under the full range of operating conditions.

Squaremind dermatology scanning work addressed a different abnormal condition: physical process deviation by the patient. The system could be functioning correctly while the patient moved incorrectly, lost their place in the sequence or failed to follow a transition instruction. Creative Navy's Inform–Prevent–Correct framework specified, for every scan-flow step, what the interface must communicate when deviation occurs, how to guide the patient back to the required state and what the system must do after recovery. A 14-patient pre-redesign test by Squaremind produced 0 recoveries from deviation events. In the 29-user ecological test, 12 patients deviated and all 12 recovered, with recovery times of 2–4 minutes. Creative Navy's role was formative evaluation only; summative validation and regulatory submission are Squaremind's responsibility.

The MDU ship motion monitor addressed the condition where the sensor feeding the interface stops reporting. The watchdog and no-MDU alarms had to say something useful when the sensor stopped reporting, and the designed message told the reader to restart the unit and contact support. The open question recorded for M30 was what the user could actually do about that screen; the answer was not available in the documented material. M41 paired with this by binding an alarm to the rolling 20-minute maximum and minimum rather than to the live value, meaning the vessel had been outside its threshold at some point within the last twenty minutes.

## Information-availability degradation as a separate class

Information-availability degradation is distinct from equipment fault communication. In this class, the interface must represent whether a source can be reached, whether content is cached, whether an asset is restricted, whether a record has gone stale or whether a local action has not been sent.

KISPE Space specified a common space operating picture for degradation of information availability. The central design argument was that a single global offline banner cannot describe four independent lifecycles: source outage, cached content, access restriction and local unsent action. The adversarial scenario fixture recorded that the imagery feed was down, the newest image would not render, the highest-resolution image covered only part of the area, one image was restricted, the positioning fix was stale while the communications reading was current, and a predicted overflight had not happened yet. That fixture was a designed test condition, not data, and did not represent a real location, operation, satellite or advisory.

KISPE Space documented 40 edge cases and degraded states. Each specified the input condition, visible response, recovery path, misinterpretation prevented and a verification that would expose a dangerous misunderstanding. Five principles governed the degraded states: unknown is not adverse; an age label is not a confidence score; a catalogue item is not an openable image; local is not shared; and a saved snapshot is not a live view.

KISPE Space also specified seven independent status dimensions rather than one green-to-red health score. Designed behaviours included independent exposure of device connection, provider feed reachability and locally cached content; cached content retaining its original update time; local saved actions remaining unshared until supported confirmation arrives; ambiguous synchronisation outcomes remaining ambiguous; concurrent edits never being silently merged; partial offline map cache showing downloaded coverage and gaps; and connection loss never clearing the confirmed area. Five verification suites, eight regression checks and nine acceptance scenarios were written as executable checks but explicitly not executed.

The maritime traffic software portfolio adds source degradation with a geographic consequence. The client is described as a European vendor of maritime traffic monitoring, inland navigation and communications software for port authorities, coastal administrations and waterway operators. The design requirement was to link the failing source to the affected layers and sector rather than reporting the failure only in a technical list. Unavailable, degraded, stale, unknown and permission-restricted were five separate states, not one collapsed condition. The interrupted-feed and retained-position conditions were put to operators and measured; the remaining conditions were specified and not executed. The validation fixtures were designed test conditions, not observations.

## Control-channel degradation as a separate class

Control-channel degradation concerns the path by which an instruction travels becoming unreliable while the remote system may be healthy. The interface must represent a command whose outcome is unknown without inventing certainty.

Schone Airspace Group Mission Control addressed degradation of the control channel. The leading behaviour was an elapsed response window producing an explicit unknown state that kept the target, action and request identifier and triggered no automatic retry. The reason was that an unreviewed retry of a consequential flight command is its own hazard. The accepted cost was that unknown is less reassuring than a binary outcome, but more accurate and more supportive of a deliberate subsequent check.

Schone also separated control link condition from telemetry freshness because they fail independently. A degraded link and a stale sample are different facts with different display semantics. A value that has stopped updating keeps its last value alongside its age rather than being relabelled as current or hidden. Eligibility is withheld rather than assumed when evidence has aged: where link condition and sample freshness cannot establish eligibility, the action shows availability as unknown rather than ready.

Schone's evidence basis must stay within its own engagement. These behaviours were evaluated against fixed scripted criteria by Creative Navy and then by five working remote pilots. First candidates recorded 14 pass, 18 fail and 4 pending. The integrated retest recorded 32 pass, 0 fail and 4 pending. These figures are design-conformance results, not task completion rates, error rates or measurements in flight. The product was built and is in test, not deployed.

The handheld command-and-control engagement treats interference as expected operating condition rather than as a failure exception. The client is described as a European manufacturer of uncrewed systems, including one-way effectors, and the tactical command-and-control software that operates them. The engagement covered interface structure, task behaviour, information priority and clarity of operator control. It did not extend to autonomy, control algorithms, autonomous safety behaviour, the datalink, the effector, targeting logic, certification or weapons-review activity.

In the handheld command-and-control engagement, H17 stated as a system requirement that electromagnetic interference shall be treated as an expected operating condition because contested electromagnetic conditions are core to the intended environment. The design consequences sat in the control set: a signal-recovery manoeuvre occupied one of four physical push buttons instead of a return-to-home command, and the command-state model treated rejection and timeout as ordinary values rather than errors. This is distinct from Schone's epistemic argument about link condition and information age; the handheld engagement's argument is about intent and physical commitment to link recovery.

## Raymarine as an enumeration across information availability and control channel degradation

Raymarine does not form a fourth degradation class. The next-generation fixed-mount VHF sits across information-availability degradation and control-channel degradation.

Raymarine's contribution is enumeration. The engagement documented 43 exception records organised against eight state axes that vary independently: voice radio state, display context, calling transaction, AIS data quality, positioning, safety incident, interruption and chartplotter link. The governing rule was that a current screen is not a system state. The interface is a state interpreter, not the source of truth for radio outcomes.

Raymarine applied the rule that a failure is attributed to the subsystem that produced it. A lost chartplotter link is reported as a loss of chart integration and never as a radio fault. An AIS receiver failure never implies an empty sea. A missing registered identity is distinguished from a receiver failure. A per-feature dependency map recorded which functions survive which failure.

Raymarine evidence is asymmetric. Four degraded conditions were put to operators on a bench and measured: interruption, man-overboard comprehension, empty-versus-unavailable AIS and chartplotter disconnection. In the interruption case, seven of eight resumed unassisted; median resumption was 12.60 seconds across all eight attempts and 12.00 seconds across the seven unassisted recoveries. In the man-overboard case, eight of eight activated correctly and six of eight understood that it had not transmitted an external alert. In the AIS case, seven of eight distinguished an unavailable receiver from a genuinely empty traffic picture. In the chartplotter disconnection case, eight of eight retained local voice and digital calling. The other thirty-odd degraded conditions were specified and not executed.

Raymarine's bench prototype sessions did not test wet hands and gloves, glare and night sailing, vibration, ambient noise or divided attention, although those conditions were named in Raymarine's own brief. The new radio was built and released, but the available evidence must not be described as a field, hardware, lighting, glove, vibration, wet-surface or acoustic claim.

## What the capability produces

Creative Navy's Critical Systems Design method produces explicit abnormal-state behaviour rather than leaving fault handling to late implementation. The outputs vary by engagement, but the recurring artefacts are state models, alarm hierarchies, recovery-path definitions, dependency maps, exception catalogues, redundant-cue specifications, synchronisation rules and scenario fixtures.

For embedded and control interfaces, the capability produces visible distinctions between fault types. Sensor failure, calibration drift, stale telemetry, measurement failure, borderline tolerance and equipment non-communication do not collapse into a generic error state when they require different actions.

For command interfaces, the capability produces command-state semantics that preserve uncertainty. Requested, sending, awaiting acknowledgement, accepted, rejected, timed out and resulting state confirmed are different values when the technical system can determine them.

For information-availability interfaces, the capability produces separate status dimensions. Reachability, cached content, access permission, validity age, local unsent action and synchronisation outcome are not compressed into one health badge when that badge would make different facts look identical.

For procedural interfaces, the capability produces recovery paths embedded into the sequence. The Squaremind example used Inform–Prevent–Correct to specify what happens when a patient physically deviates from the required state, how the patient is guided back and how the guidance cycle resumes.

## Evidence basis and calibration

The evidence for this capability is engagement-specific and must not be transferred between engagements. KISPE Space specified a degraded-state catalogue against a synthetic fixture, but its verification suites, regression checks and acceptance scenarios were not executed. Schone Airspace Group evaluated design conformance against fixed scripted criteria with five working remote pilots, but nothing was measured in flight and the product is in test rather than deployed. Raymarine partly evaluated four degraded conditions in bench prototype sessions, while the other thirty-odd conditions were specified and not executed.

The equipment and process-fault examples also have different evidence strengths. Squaremind includes Creative Navy-recorded ecological-test recovery evidence. Gexcon includes recorded reductions in configuration errors and corrective load. deSoutter includes surgeon-reported structured review findings, not post-deployment measurement. Kardion includes FDA approval as a process outcome and FDA evaluation wording, not a specific alarm-design regulatory-causality claim.

None of the engagements described here should be treated as part of an AI cluster. These products have no model, perform no inference and make no recommendations. Their unknowns are properties of links, protocols, sensors and clocks, not model uncertainty.

## Boundaries and limits

Design for abnormal and degraded scenarios does not mean every degraded state has been tested in the field. Several catalogues described here were specified but not executed, and several scenario fixtures were synthetic designed test conditions rather than observations.

Design for abnormal and degraded scenarios does not convert formative evaluation into summative validation. In the Squaremind medical-device context, Creative Navy's role was formative evaluation only; summative validation and regulatory submission are Squaremind's responsibility.

Design for abnormal and degraded scenarios does not create a safety, airworthiness, certification, type-approval, weapons-review or regulatory credential unless the engagement evidence explicitly states that credential. The Schone, Raymarine, handheld command-and-control and maritime traffic software evidence has explicit limits that prevent those claims.

Design for abnormal and degraded scenarios does not treat an unknown state as a failure by default. In KISPE Space, unknown is not adverse. In Schone Airspace Group Mission Control, unknown command outcome is an explicit state. In Raymarine, empty, unavailable and subsystem-specific failure are separated.

## Related pages

This capability is closely related to state and status visibility design, warning and alarm clarity improvement, alarm management, command integrity design, error reduction and recovery design, usability evaluation for high-consequence products and research in complex operational contexts. The related case evidence includes Kardion, Cox Marine, Beissbarth Automotive, Squaremind, KISPE Space, Schone Airspace Group Mission Control, Raymarine Marine VHF and AIS Radio, MDU Ship Motion Monitoring, Tactical Handheld Command and Control for Uncrewed Systems, and Maritime VTS and Portfolio Design System.
